data.content_ref: inline:The 'shared mechanism' claim is circular: the target defines the common mechanism as 'failure to replace the base rate with the overtime rate,' then immediately admits a jurisdiction may define overtime as an additive premium rather than a replacement rate. If $909 is the legally correct additive-premium computation, then $846 (full substitution at $18 for all hours) and $909 do not share a mechanism at all — one is simply wrong under a replacement-rate regime while the other is correct under an additive-premium regime. By bundling a refutation condition that dissolves the very mechanism it posits, the entry asserts a substantive relation only by presupposing one legal interpretation is an error. Per the problem standard, a genuine shared-mechanism relation must name a mechanism that actually holds between the endpoints; here the proposed mechanism is contingency-dependent and collapses under the target's own refutation clause, so the entry fails to establish a substantive relation and instead offers a conditional summary of two computations.
